subject.title: A View from Cannery Row, Monterey
subject.author: Thomas Kinkade

title: The Industry That Built This View Collapsed Overnight. So Did His.
standfirst: Thomas Kinkade painted Cannery Row in 1996, half a century after the sardines that built it vanished from Monterey Bay in a single season. He then built a business on the same principle that had wrecked the place — extract fast, sell wide, assume the supply holds — and watched it fail the same way.

sections.heading: A Row Built on a Fish That Disappeared
sections.body: Monterey's cannery district began in 1902, when the packer Frank Booth converted a failing salmon operation to process sardines instead. Demand exploded during the First World War, when France's own sardine exports stopped and American canners filled the gap. By the early 1940s, more than thirty canneries lined what was still called Ocean View Avenue, employing three to four thousand people — nearly half the town — drawn from Sicilian, Japanese, Portuguese and Chinese immigrant communities. Then, after 1946, the sardines themselves collapsed: overfishing, a shift in ocean temperature and the fish's own boom-and-bust cycle emptied the bay within a few seasons. The last cannery, Hovden, did not close until 1973, but John Steinbeck had already fixed the place in fiction by then, opening his 1945 novel by calling it, in one breath, [a poem, a stink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannery_Row), a grating noise, a quality of light, a tone, a habit, a nostalgia, a dream — a description written while the canneries were still working, and still smelled like it.

sections.heading: Rebuilt as a Memory of Itself
sections.body: What Kinkade painted fifty years later was not a working waterfront but a resurrection of one. The street was renamed Cannery Row only in 1958, after Steinbeck's novel had made the old name more famous than the place itself, and the abandoned canneries were gradually converted into restaurants, hotels and gift shops trading on the grit the novel described and the neighbourhood had since scrubbed off. The largest of these conversions is the [Monterey Bay Aquarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannery_Row), opened in 1984 directly on the site of the old Hovden cannery — the last one standing, repurposed rather than demolished. By the time Kinkade set up his easel in 1996, Cannery Row had already completed the transformation his painting takes for granted: from an industrial slum built on an extracted resource, to a themed re-creation of itself, sold to visitors as heritage.

sections.heading: The Man Behind the Light
sections.body: Kinkade — born William Thomas Kinkade III, in Sacramento County on 19 January 1958 — grew up poor in nearby Placerville, raised by a single mother in a house that regularly went without heat or electricity. He studied at UC Berkeley before transferring to the ArtCenter College of Design in Pasadena, where the painters Charles Bell and Glenn Wessels mentored him. In the summer of 1980 he crossed the country sketching with a fellow art student, James Gurney; the book the two produced from the trip, The Artist's Guide to Sketching, became a bestseller in 1982. Both men then went to work for [Ralph Bakshi's studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Kinkade), painting background art for the animated film Fire and Ice — the job in which, by his own later account, Kinkade first started thinking seriously about how to paint light.

sections.heading: An Industry of His Own
sections.body: The Painter of Light™ business began with a decision not to sell paintings, in the ordinary sense, at all. A backer named Ken Raasch set up a company to reproduce Kinkade's originals as lithographs and canvas transfers, tiered by price — plain print, canvas transfer, print hand-touched by a paid assistant, print hand-touched by Kinkade himself — and [taken public in 1994](https://hyperallergic.com/the-mystery-of-the-painter-of-light/). By 1996, the year of this painting, a single Kinkade image might be printed in an edition of 100,000. The reproductions moved through Hallmark calendars and puzzles, QVC, and a growing network of franchised Thomas Kinkade Signature Galleries, each contractually bound to the company's own décor, pricing and stock. The company later claimed that [one in every twenty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Kinkade) American homes owned a copy of something he had painted.

sections.heading: When the Extraction Caught Up With Him
sections.body: The gallery network ran, for a while, on the same logic as the old canneries: keep taking, and assume the supply holds. The company undercut its own franchisees by dumping unsold prints through liquidators and selling near-identical editions more cheaply on QVC, while continuing to sell new franchise licences into markets already saturated. Owners went bankrupt on inventory nobody wanted. In 2006 an arbitration panel awarded two of them, Karen Hazlewood and Jeffrey Spinello, $2.8 million after finding the company had withheld material information, and [the FBI opened an investigation](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/amp/wbna14576181) into the franchise sales that same August. By June 2010, Kinkade's own manufacturing arm, Pacific Metro, was in Chapter 11 bankruptcy, owing $6.2 million. The galleries had gone the way of the canneries: a resource oversold until it stopped paying out.

sections.heading: The Painter of Light, After Dark
sections.body: Kinkade insisted he was misunderstood rather than cynical. "I am really the most controversial artist in the world," he said in 2001, and elsewhere compared himself to Andy Warhol — "my hero, and I'm his heir apparent" — apparently without irony about which part of Warhol's career he meant. Critics were rarely so generous: Joan Didion once described his signature glow as producing cottages of "such insistent coziness as to seem actually sinister," and after his death the critic Nathan Rabin called his career ["the triumph of sub-mediocrity."](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Kinkade) Kinkade died at his home in Monte Sereno on 6 April 2012, aged 54; an autopsy found acute alcohol and diazepam intoxication, two years after a drink-driving arrest near Carmel had already put the gap between the public glow and the private man on the record. A 2023 documentary went looking through roughly six hundred of some six thousand paintings he had never shown anyone — dark, unpublished charcoal work its makers described as "darkness that lurked inside of him." None of it looked like Cannery Row.
